02 / Workflows

Follow the work.

Use AI to reach further while keeping the important thinking yours. Our developing learning framework starts with a first attempt and ends with a result you can defend.

Think and delegate

Write your goal, first idea, and what a good result would look like. Choose what AI should help with: a hint, a critique, a comparison, or execution you know how to check.

Inspect and explain

Look for assumptions, missing evidence, and parts you do not understand. Explain the key idea in your own words with the chat closed.

Verify and own

Check the result against a source, a calculation, a test, or the actual behavior. Decide what to keep or change, and identify what you contributed.

Choose the assistance

When learning a skill, start with hints or feedback on your attempt. Give an agent more responsibility when you understand the task and can spot a failure.

Try it · A small design exerciseOne revision. A reason for every change.Use AI as a critic, then check whether your own revision solves the problem.

03 / New capabilities

Find out what changed.

A new model or tool matters when it changes something you can actually do. Compare it on a real task: the quality of the result, the mistakes you catch, and the effort needed to get something usable.

For a first test, choose a short task with a clear success condition. Keep the task and constraints the same across tools, inspect both results, and record where each needed correction. One comparison is a starting point, not a permanent ranking.

Do / First experiment

Make a revision you can defend.

Choose a slide, poster, or page you made. Use a copy and remove personal information before sharing it with an AI tool. Follow the AI-use rules for any school work.

Start with your judgment

Write who it is for, what they should understand, and one thing that feels unclear. Make your own first revision before asking for feedback.

Ask for a critique

Try: “The audience is [audience], and the main idea is [idea]. Identify the single biggest obstacle to understanding it. Explain why. Do not redesign it for me.”

Choose one change

Compare the critique with your own diagnosis. Accept, adapt, or reject it with a reason. Make one focused change and keep the original beside it.

Check the result

Show both versions to someone without explaining your intent. Ask what they understood first. Then close the chat and explain why your change helped—or why it needs another attempt.

This is a starter exercise, not a measured learning intervention. The useful result is a clearer artifact and a decision you can explain.
